agent.name: Emerging Technology Diffusion Agent
agent.specialty: Rogers diffusion, application and peer diffusion, and bounded organizational timing

analytical_question: As of the 2026-11-01 evidence snapshot, how far has LLM-based generative AI diffused generally, and how far has clinician-reviewed note drafting/summarization diffused among comparable hospitals, specialties and EHR workflows? For a hypothetical risk-sensitive hospital with a six-month planning horizon from the 2026-11-01 test date, what evidence and prerequisites condition timing of a documentation-only evaluation? Adoption units must be distinguished: individual technical worker, clinician, clinical team and hospital with authorized sustained use. Geography, jurisdiction, peer denominator and routine-use definition are unspecified.
general_et_finding: The shared evidence demonstrates actual reported AI use, not merely product access: E1-C1 reports 90% individual current workplace AI use among surveyed technology professionals in 2025; E1-C2 reports that 60% of surveyed AI users used AI about half the time or more on encountered tasks in a retrospective three-month window. E4-C1 reports 75.9% of 2024 technical/professional survey respondents relied partly on AI for at least one daily responsibility, and E4-C2 reports 74.9% within the subset whose jobs involve writing code relied partly on AI for coding. These are broad-AI, respondent-based, sector-focused observations with distinct denominators and dates, not LLM-only rates or authorized company deployments. E2 repeats E4 historical data, not a new independent prevalence observation; its team incorporation is perceived team-work share, not enterprise counts. D1-D3 describe historical access, developer integrations or medical-model availability; none measures population adoption. E3 supplies bounded student use-practice themes, not prevalence. The adoption ladder remains awareness (unmeasured), access/trial (described but conversion unmeasured), individual current use (E1/E4), self-reported recurring/task-frequency use (E1/E4), sustained authorized organizational use (unmeasured), and industry institutional penetration (unmeasured). Within Rogers’ timing framework, innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority and laggards are relative to a defined social system and actual adoption timing. Substantial surveyed technical-worker use is compatible with adoption beyond isolated innovators in that sampled setting, but biased cross-sectional broad-AI data do not assign a defensible exact category, percentage split, chasm crossing, S-curve, saturation, global LLM stage or current hospital stage. The 2024 and 2025 observations are historical and exceed the proposed 12-month review flag as of November 2026; no longitudinal trend can be computed by comparing them.
application_finding: Application boundary: LLM drafting or summarizing notes for clinician review, not diagnosis, prescribing, treatment, autonomous chart entry or approval. Neither E1/E4 technical-worker adoption nor E4 coding-task reliance measures clinical-documentation use. D3 establishes existence of a medical-model ecosystem, not clinician utilization, ambient-scribe deployment or hospital-level penetration. Relevant peers are similarly situated hospitals in a specified jurisdiction, clinical specialties and comparable EHR/documentation workflows; institutional pilots, purchases, licensed seats, clinician current use and sustained authorized routine use require separate measures. No representative direct peer rate, numerator, denominator, observation period or current hospital adoption stage is supplied. Five diffusion characteristics follow; their directions are hypotheses for this application rather than measured clinical effects. Relative advantage: no direct quality-adjusted documentation time/cost/accuracy evidence; effect unknown or mixed because drafting could reduce writing burden but review, corrections and omissions could offset it; condition is measured baseline and independent note-quality, time and rework outcomes, confidence low. Compatibility: no verified EHR/workflow/privacy/consent compatibility; likely inhibitory until demonstrated because sensitive patient information, clinician attestation, established documentation conventions and jurisdiction-specific rules constrain use; condition is local clinical, privacy and EHR approval, confidence low for outcome and moderate for scenario constraint. Complexity: no measured hospital integration/training burden; likely inhibitory or mixed because prompt management, EHR mapping, verification of omissions, training, auditing and escalation add workload despite convenient text generation; condition is measured integration, clinician review and exception-handling effort, confidence low. Trialability: D3 describes developer notebooks/model access, not an authorized clinical pilot; potentially accelerating only for a reversible, bounded, approved evaluation using permitted data, with clinician oversight and stop criteria; real permissions, setup cost, isolation and rollback unknown, confidence low. Observability: no direct verified clinical outcomes or comparable-hospital routine-use figures; presently inhibitory/unknown because demos and vendor claims are not trusted clinical evidence, though auditable blinded note-quality and clinician-workload results could improve visibility; condition is predefined outcomes, peer reporting and transparent error monitoring, confidence low. Diffusion mechanisms: D3 supports an issuer-described supplier/developer channel, but its ability to accelerate hospital diffusion is inference. Possible change agents are clinical informatics leaders and privacy/EHR implementation teams; possible opinion leaders are respected clinicians in relevant specialties, verified through actual peer communication and demonstrated evaluation credibility, not invented endorsements. Procurement vendors, specialty societies, peer networks, professional meetings, interoperable EHR tools, training and governance may transmit trial knowledge; standardization and interoperability in this setting are not proven by a README/API. Potential accelerator is an approved small reversible test plus trusted peer outcomes; inhibitors include privacy/security review, error consequences, EHR incompatibility, governance and staff-time limits. Their effect magnitudes and hospital prevalence are not established.
organization_specific_finding: The hospital and its conservative, risk-sensitive posture are fixed hypothetical case descriptors; an established EHR, formal governance and constrained clinician attention are stated scenario assumptions, not observed facts. Conservatism signals a higher evidence threshold and preference for accountable, reversible learning; without relative adoption timestamps and a hospital peer distribution it does not establish late-majority or laggard Rogers status. No current local use, comparative peer rank, jurisdiction, specialty mix, permissions, EHR integration, procurement capacity, budget, staffing or baseline workload is reported. Clinical record omissions, sensitive information and downstream care risks make documentation application-specific uncertainty consequential, while the general technical-worker evidence stays unchanged. Over the assumed six-month horizon, first clarify permitted note types and clinical owners and collect baseline and peer denominators; consider only a governance-approved, bounded clinician-reviewed evaluation if privacy, interoperability, data provenance, human review, independent quality measures and rollback controls are established. A later expansion discussion would require repeated observed authorized use and acceptable quality-adjusted workload and safety outcomes against management-set criteria. Unresolved governance, unreliable notes, excess verification burden, privacy incidents or lack of clinical authority delay or reverse that timing option; inability to trial now does not establish nonuse or mandate waiting indefinitely.

evidence.claim: E1-C1: 90% of surveyed technology professionals reported using AI at work; individual current-use measure, not LLM-only or hospital adoption.
evidence.date_or_recency: Published 2025 (September report release per issuer); 2025 survey context, exact fieldwork dates unavailable; historical and flagged for refresh as of 2026-11-01.
evidence.evidence_type: Original issuer survey infographic and inspected questionnaire; cross-sectional self-report
evidence.notes: Nearly 5,000 technology professionals worldwide; exact item n, recruitment and weighting for 2025 not reported in supplied evidence. Broad AI wording. DORA/Google Cloud affiliation and self-report limit representativeness. Panel 01 and instrument current-use item; not a count of hospitals or authorized enterprise deployments.

evidence.claim: E1-C2: 60% of surveyed AI users reported using AI about half the time or more when encountering a task/problem over the preceding three months; individual retrospective task-frequency measure.
evidence.date_or_recency: Published 2025; three-month recall within 2025 survey context; exact fieldwork dates not reported; refresh flag as of 2026-11-01.
evidence.evidence_type: Original issuer cross-sectional self-report frequency item
evidence.notes: Denominator is surveyed AI users, not all professionals, developers, firms or clinicians; item n unavailable. Panel 04 and instrument. Does not measure daily active use, persistent retention, LLM-only activity or organizational authorization. Same E1 source, not independent validation.

evidence.claim: E4-C1 and E4-C2: In 2024, 75.9% of survey respondents reported partial AI reliance for at least one daily work responsibility; among respondents whose responsibilities include coding, 74.9% reported partial AI reliance for writing code.
evidence.date_or_recency: 2024 report, version 2024.3; 2024 observation period, exact field dates and release day unavailable; older than 12-month refresh flag.
evidence.evidence_type: Original cross-sectional survey, methodological sections inspected
evidence.notes: Nearly 3,000 working professionals from 104 countries overall; per-item n unavailable. Organic blog/email/social/snowball recruitment plus supplementary panels; three survey flows. The 74.9% denominator is coding-responsibility respondents, not all workers. Pages 19, 91, 97, 102. Self-selection and broad AI wording; neither rate measures hospital documentation or sustained institutional use.

evidence.claim: E2-C1 to E2-C3: A 2025 publication repeats rounded 76% AI reliance from the 2024 sample, defines team incorporation through respondent-estimated share of team work supported by AI over three months, and proposes license/DAU telemetry without reporting it as collected impact evidence.
evidence.date_or_recency: Released March 2025 per issuer; version 2025.2; based on 2024 survey and September 2024 interviews, not a 2025 prevalence sample.
evidence.evidence_type: Issuer analytical report reusing E4 observational data; qualitative interviews and Bayesian modeling
evidence.notes: Underlying nearly 3,000 professional respondents from 104 countries; separate ten development-professional interviews in September 2024. Team measure uses perceived share of work, not hospital or company share. Printed pages 3, 30, 37, 41. Not independent replication of E4, randomized causal proof, or audited deployment; 2024 methods cannot be transplanted into E1 2025.

evidence.claim: E3-C1: Participating students describe moderating AI assistance, verifying generated work and worrying about dependence and skill development; contextual evidence for a possible verification/trust mechanism only.
evidence.date_or_recency: Published and updated 2026-02-17; eight-month project, exact fieldwork dates not reported.
evidence.evidence_type: Original issuer-reported student mixed-methods qualitative findings
evidence.notes: UC Berkeley EECS, Design and Data Science participants; participant n and sampling frame not reported. Interviews/survey responses, no representative prevalence denominator. Student coding context cannot establish clinician preferences, hospital adoption, or safety outcomes. Mechanism transfer is only a hypothesis.

evidence.claim: D1: Archived GitHub Copilot preview README states product general availability, a historical coding-assistant commercialization/access signal, not an adoption count.
evidence.date_or_recency: Original publication undated; retrieved 2026-11-02T00:51:23.545126+00:00; linked announcement URL includes 2022-06-21 but announcement not inspected.
evidence.evidence_type: Issuer technical README, historical product description
evidence.notes: No sampled population, adoption denominator, observation period, trial-conversion or ongoing-use metric. Possible ecosystem/access accelerator is inference only. Shares GitHub/Microsoft ecosystem with D2, not independent replication. Not clinical documentation evidence.

evidence.claim: D2: Archived Microsoft VS Code Copilot Chat README describes inline suggestions, chat, agent workflows, free sign-up, enterprise administration and extension/version dependencies.
evidence.notes: Access/integration channels may aid coding-tool trial and compatibility; update/admin dependencies may inhibit it. Archived vendor-authored README, no validated present pricing/performance, user denominator, actual adoption or causal effect. No inference to clinical EHR interoperability.

evidence.claim: D3: Google Health MedGemma repository describes medical text/image model variants, notebooks, access links and licensing separation; establishes model ecosystem existence only.
evidence.notes: Potential complementary assets for development or bounded experimentation are inferred. No hospital sample, clinical-documentation use definition, ambient-scribe rollouts, outcome validation, independent benchmark confirmation, EHR compatibility, regulatory authorization or sustained-use denominator. Linked model card and evaluations not inspected.

contrary_evidence_or_limitations: The claim “most comparable hospitals now routinely use LLM-assisted clinical documentation” has no original representative hospital-level routine-use survey, geographic frame, specialty/workflow stratification, numerator, denominator or sustained-deployment measure in the supplied snapshot. Absence of such evidence does not prove nonadoption.

E1 and E4 do document substantial individual technical-worker AI use, but their broad-AI wording, nonhospital respondents and separate denominators block extrapolation to LLM-only clinical documentation or institutional penetration.

E1 2025 fieldwork and recruitment/weighting details are missing; E4 2024 recruitment is partly self-selected; per-item n is unavailable. Both exceed the analyst 12-month refresh flag by November 2026.

E2 reanalyzes E4 2024 material; rounded 76% is not independent of E4-C1 75.9%. Team-work incorporation is respondent perception, not an audited hospital count; observational models do not establish causal quality or productivity effects.
E3 is a 2026 publication about bounded student observations with undisclosed n and exact field dates; it cannot update professional/hospital prevalence or verify clinician behavior.

D3 medical-model descriptions and uninspected evaluation links provide neither ambient-scribe clinical trial results nor validated safety, regulatory compliance or routine hospital use. D1 and D2 belong to a related coding ecosystem and do not measure EHR adoption.
Unavailable original healthcare/AMA, PubMed, ASTP/ONC, Stack Overflow, METR and full 2025 DORA methods routes were excluded. No findings are inferred from their titles or access errors.

No local quality-adjusted time, error, rework, clinician acceptability, data-handling permission, authorized sustained use or comparable-hospital peer sample is provided. No precise adoption stage, date to mainstream adoption or causal savings estimate can be supported.
confidence_and_uncertainty: Moderate confidence that inspected original DORA documents report substantial self-reported individual AI use in their surveyed technical-worker samples and that D1-D3 describe product/model channels; lower confidence that these nonprobability and broad-AI estimates represent all LLM use in 2026. Low confidence in any clinical-documentation application diffusion, peer stage or hospital rank: no direct hospital adoption evidence. Low empirical but conditional scenario-based confidence in organizational timing: risk and governance mechanisms are plausible, but actual EHR, permissions, quality, capacity and management thresholds are unknown. Source existence/issuer wording is more certain than external generalizability or causal claims. Observation dates differ from publication and 2026-11-02 retrieval; 2024/2025 figures require fresh measurement.
value_opportunity_implication: A clinician-reviewed documentation aid could create value through reduced note-writing effort or improved workflow, but this is an unverified application hypothesis. Evaluate total quality-adjusted clinician time including review/rework, completeness and error consequences, user experience and resource costs relative to an observed baseline. Do not translate technical-worker survey use, medical-model availability or generated text speed into hospital ROI, saved hours or adoption probability.
risk_governance_implication: Limit the analytical scope to drafting/summarization with a licensed, accountable clinician retaining responsibility for verification and final records. Before any real clinical use, relevant hospital authorities must review patient-data handling, jurisdiction-specific consent/privacy requirements, access controls, vendor/data flows, provenance, logging, retention, EHR interoperability, clinical safety criteria and incident/rollback processes. Clinician review is necessary in the scenario but not proven sufficient to prevent omissions or downstream harm. This agent neither certifies compliance nor authorizes deployment.
recommendation_management_implication: For the six-month hypothetical planning horizon, initiate a documentation-use definition and evidence inventory now, led by named clinical/informatics, privacy/security, quality and EHR accountable owners to be assigned locally. Measure baseline note time, rework, error types and clinician burden and seek dated comparable-hospital evidence. Only if authorized privacy/data/EHR and clinician-review gates are met should management consider a small reversible evaluation on approved workflows with predefined patient-safety, note-quality, time and stop criteria; any schedule or threshold is a management proposal, not a measured benchmark. A subsequent stage depends on repeated auditable use and acceptable outcomes plus decision-owner approval; adverse quality, weak integration, unacceptable burden or unresolved permissions postpone or reverse the timing. The Adoption Agent and accountable human/clinical leadership retain the integrated adoption decision.
change_monitoring_triggers: Clinical informatics and records leadership: document target specialty, note types, eligible clinicians, routine-use definition, jurisdiction and actual local baseline; revisit at initial gate and again within the proposed six-month planning horizon.

Privacy/security and legal/compliance candidate owners: verify approved data access, consent/permissions where applicable, vendor terms, retention, security, audit and incident handling; reassess at any material change or before handling real patient data.

EHR/informatics candidate owner: demonstrate approved integration, note provenance, clinician sign-off, recoverability and reversible shutdown before a limited evaluation; any failed test pauses progression.

Clinical quality/safety and evaluation candidate owners: prespecify and repeatedly measure note omissions, inaccuracies, corrections, clinician review time, total documentation time, workflow disruption, incidents and patient-safety escalation in any authorized evaluation; management sets thresholds beforehand.

Research/strategy candidate owner: obtain a dated original representative hospital documentation survey or administrative dataset with hospital denominator, geography, specialty, pilot versus authorized routine-use distinction, repeated-use duration and methods; refresh 2024/2025 technical-worker evidence before reusing it as current.

Hospital clinical champion and management candidate owners: assess credible same-specialty peer experience, uptake/repeated eligible-clinician use and staff acceptability, and hold a formally scheduled evidence-gate review within six months or sooner after a significant safety, privacy or interoperability event.
abstention_or_more_information_needed: Abstain from asserting that most comparable hospitals routinely use LLM-assisted clinical documentation or assigning a numerical hospital market penetration or Rogers stage. Request a dated original representative hospital-level survey or administrative source with geography, comparable specialty/workflow sampling frame, exact institution denominator, routine/authorized-use definition, collection dates and longitudinal persistence.

Abstain from determining this hospital’s peer rank or labeling it late majority/laggard. Request comparable institutional first-use dates, stages of adoption, governance status, denominators and the hospital’s own dated deployment record.

Abstain from inferring hospital prevalence from E1/E4 AI-worker self-reports, E2 team-work perceptions or D3 medical model access. Request clinician- and hospital-specific documentation-use evidence separating awareness, access, trial, current use, repeated authorized use and sustained institutional coverage.

Abstain from specifying actual trial start, safe scope, regulatory compliance or deployment authority. Request jurisdiction, EHR interfaces, approved data permissions and clinician oversight protocol, specialty/note types, information-security review and accountable decision owners.

Abstain from any estimated causal productivity, quality, safety or ROI magnitude and forecast date for mainstream adoption. Request local baseline and approved comparative evaluation of quality-adjusted time, omissions, rework, clinician burden, meaningful retention and costs, plus updated longitudinal and peer evidence.

Also qualify the generic claim that most comparable software firms sustain company-wide coding-assistant deployments; the available individual technical-worker observations lack enterprise denominators, authorization and repeated use telemetry. This caveat does not establish hospital adoption.
